canonicalExplanation.summary: A Python `str` is a sequence of **Unicode code points**, not bytes and not always "one visible letter each". Build text with **f-strings** and `"sep".join(parts)`, compare user text with `.casefold()` (stronger than `.lower()`), and convert to **bytes** with `.encode("utf-8")` only at the edge — when writing a file or sending over a network.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.body:
Your sales report must show names like "José" and "Zoë", line up columns, and save to a file every spreadsheet can open. Meanwhile a login check says "STRASSE" and "straße" don't match. Text has rules worth knowing. A report builds rows with join and f-strings, then encodes UTF-8 only at the file or network boundary. In this lesson you'll implement and test robust text normalization, parsing and formatting.

```predict
{"question": "What is `f\"{name:<6}|{qty:>3}\"` for `name = \"tea\"`, `qty = 5`?", "options": ["\"tea   |  5\"", "\"tea|5\""], "answer": 0, "why": "`:<6` left-aligns in 6 characters; `:>3` right-aligns in 3. f-string format specs line up columns."}
```

sections.heading: Before you begin
sections.body: You should know **for, while and loop control**, **Data-structure choice**, **Numbers, booleans, None and text**, and **Lists, tuples and slicing** — strings are sequences too.

sections.heading: The model: text inside, bytes at the boundary
sections.body:
```python
rows = [("José", 3), ("Zoë", 12)]
lines = [f"{name:<6}{qty:>4}" for name, qty in rows]
report = "\n".join(lines)              # still str

with open("report.txt", "w", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    f.write(report)                       # encoded at the boundary
```

| Task | Tool |
|---|---|
| format one row. | f-string with specs. |
| combine many pieces. | `"sep".join(list)`. |
| split input. | `.split(",")`, `.strip()`. |
| compare case-insensitively. | `.casefold()`. |
| text → bytes. | `.encode("utf-8")`, only at I/O. |

```reveal
{"prompt": "Why `\"\\n\".join(lines)` instead of `report += line` in a loop?", "answer": "join builds the result in one go and makes the separator explicit. Repeated `+=` creates a new string each time and is easy to get wrong."}
```

sections.heading: One character isn't always one glyph
sections.body:
```predict
{"question": "`s = \"e\\u0301\"` displays as \"é\". What is `len(s)`?", "options": ["1", "2"], "answer": 1, "why": "It's two code points: `e` plus a combining accent. Use `unicodedata.normalize(\"NFC\", s)` to combine them before comparing or counting."}
```

And `"STRASSE".casefold() == "straße".casefold()` is True, while `.lower()` gives False.

examples.title: Building a UTF-8 report
examples.situation: A report builds rows with join and f-strings, then encodes UTF-8 only at the file or network boundary.
walkthrough: **Build rows with f-strings:** `f"{name:<6}{qty:>4}"` formats "José" and "Zoë" into aligned columns.
**Join:** `"\n".join(lines)` combines the rows into one str, still Unicode text.
**Encode at the file boundary:** `open(..., "w", encoding="utf-8")` writes the text as UTF-8 bytes.
examples.result: The report shows accented names correctly and opens as UTF-8 in any editor.

examples.title: The login that ignored capitals wrong
examples.situation: A sign-in compares `typed.lower() == stored.lower()`. A German user typed "STRASSE"; the stored name is "straße".
walkthrough: `.casefold()` maps ß to "ss", so both become "strasse".
Fix: normalise with NFC, then compare `.casefold()` values; add a test with this pair.
examples.result: With normalization and casefold, the two spellings compare equal and the test passes.

misconceptions.mistakenBelief: One Python character is always one displayed glyph, and calling lower makes arbitrary Unicode text safely comparable.
misconceptions.correction: A str holds code points; one visible glyph can be several code points, so normalize (NFC) first. For case-insensitive comparison use casefold, which handles cases like ß that lower misses.
misconceptions.diagnosticPrompt: In "The login that ignored capitals wrong", why didn't lower() work?

analogy.example: Think of str as **spoken words** and bytes as **a recording on tape**. You edit the words freely; you only choose a tape format (UTF-8) when you save or send it.
usefulFor: remembering to keep text as str until I/O
limitations: Recordings lose nothing with UTF-8; some older encodings can't store every character.
Combining accents have no clean spoken-word equivalent.
